Why I still carry a paper notebook

Every gadget I own promises to remember things for me. The one that works costs three pounds.

Marcus Oyelaran

I have tried every note-taking app there is. I have synced, tagged, filed and searched. I have set up systems with folders inside folders, and I have abandoned every one of them within a month. The notebook in my jacket pocket, a cheap one with a soft cover and squared paper, has outlasted them all.

Part of the reason is speed. By the time a phone has woken up, recognised my face and opened the right app, the thought I wanted to write down has usually wandered off. A notebook opens at the last page I used, and a pencil never needs charging.

But the bigger reason is that paper forgets in a useful way. An app keeps everything forever, perfectly searchable, which means it keeps all the half-ideas and shopping lists with the same weight as the things that mattered. When a notebook fills up, I read it through before starting the next one, and I copy out only what still seems worth keeping. The rest quietly goes on a shelf.

Paper forgets in a useful way.

That small ritual of copying turns out to be where most of my thinking happens. Writing something out a second time forces me to decide whether I believe it. Half of what I scribbled in a hurry does not survive the trip to the new notebook, and I do not miss it.

There is also something to be said for a tool that does one thing. My notebook does not tell me about the news, and it does not buzz when someone likes a photograph. When I open it on the train, I am only ever writing.

I am not against screens. I read on one most evenings, and I would not want to go back to a world without search. But for the first rough version of an idea, the fragile moment before it has a shape, I have found nothing better than a few square centimetres of paper and something to make a mark with.

So when people ask what app I use to stay organised, I reach into my pocket and show them. They usually laugh. Then, quite often, a few weeks later, they tell me they have bought one too.

Marcus Oyelaran is a writer and teacher. His column appears every other Saturday.
